title: On a horizon's null plane the canonical part of a spacetime-algebra spinor is the image of Lambda(m), two complex channels, one per chirality, with helicity about the generators equal to minus the chirality; so, given one (Q) version 3 array per complex channel, one massless Dirac species supplies two arrays per light ray (ln 2 at the Hawking temperature) and one Weyl field one
text: The series counts quantum modes on a black hole's horizon, and it needs each counted unit to hold exactly one bit of entropy. With its current assumption about the modes' energies, one ladder of modes holds half a bit, so a counted unit must be two ladders, and nothing explained why. This result traces the ladders to the particles that would carry them. Particles of spin one half, like electrons and neutrinos, are described by spinors. On the surface swept out by the horizon's light rays only half of a spinor's components carry particles across it, and those split into two channels, the two handednesses of the particle, with the spin about the light rays fixed by the handedness. So a spin-one-half particle that has both handednesses, as the electron does, supplies exactly two ladders per light ray, one bit; a particle with one handedness only supplies half a bit. The horizon's total is then counted in bits, two ladders to a bit, over all its fields.

title: Quantised as an elementary field with $i = I_{4}$, the rung field is linear on all eight real components of the complexified rung summand, and on that summand (on values, not on spacetime points) the hypercharge rotation is the rung boost at $I_{4}$-imaginary rapidity; besides the stored neutral mode and charged pair it carries a neutral normal pair, the directions that change $Q$, of mass squared $2W' + 4N(k_{10} \pm r)$, and the null-lift constraint is the limit $k_{10} \to \infty$; under the Gildener-Weinberg formula and decoupling the normal pair enters the scalon sum (the standard two-doublet sum rule), so the charged pair lies below $456$ GeV (below $383$ GeV when the normal pair is the heavier), the normal pair below $542$ GeV, and $h \to \gamma\gamma$ below $0.900$ of the Standard Model rate for every charged mass between $m_{h}/2$ and $456$ GeV
text: To treat the series' Higgs candidate, the rung field, as a quantum field one has to say what its quantum values are. The series' own imaginary unit, the spacetime volume element, works for it, and with that unit the hypercharge symmetry turns out to be the series' frame boost taken at imaginary speed. A quantum field of the ordinary, well-behaved kind cannot be confined to the curved surface on which the rung field was defined; it has to range over all its directions, and two extra neutral particles appear, the directions off the surface. If the weak scale arises from quantum corrections alone, as an earlier result explored, these two particles must be counted: the charged scalar that result predicted near 450 GeV is then lighter, the new neutral pair lies below about 540 GeV, and the predicted shortfall in the Higgs boson's decays to two photons, about ten per cent, remains for every allowed charged mass. (Since 2 November 2026 that quantum-corrections route is recorded as ruled out under the series' reading of how the Higgs field couples to quarks: the measured two-photon rate lies well above the predicted shortfall, the new neutral pair would make bottom mesons turn into their antiparticles far faster than is observed, and the forces among these particles would grow too strong within a few TeV. The working alternative has the second set of particles at a few TeV.)

title: The curvature-independence clause (Loc) is independent of the Clausius relation, of (R$_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and of every $\Lambda$-vacuum horizon datum of the store; a density $\tfrac14(1 + c\,S_{ab}S^{ab})$ passes all of them and differs from $\tfrac14$ in the Einstein static universe, and on the integrated reading such failures are confined to spacetimes with no calibrated vacuum point
text: To derive Einstein's equations from thermodynamics one assumes that every small piece of horizon carries the same entropy per unit area, whatever the gravitational field strength or matter there. Could that follow from the rest of the series? This result says no, by example. Imagine a world where the entropy per area is a quarter plus a small extra amount that grows with the matter-induced part of the gravitational field strength. Around black holes and in empty space with a cosmological constant that extra amount is zero, so every black-hole and cosmological-horizon fact the series relies on is unchanged. But in a universe uniformly filled with dust it is not zero, and the heat-balance argument still works there, just with a slightly different strength of gravity. So the equal-entropy-everywhere assumption is doing real work: it is what fixes how strongly matter sources the gravitational field, and the rest of the series does not supply it.

title: On local Rindler horizons and small diamonds, clauses (ii) and (iii) of (C$_{\mathrm{loc}}$), with (iii) read on the patch's whole mode algebra and the boost acting on the modes by phases, are one condition, joint KMS for the local boost at rapidity period $2\pi$, the period at which the local boost's Euclidean section is regular at leading order
text: The assumption that every small horizon is hot at the Unruh temperature and that its quantum state's internal clock runs along the horizon's own boost was stated as two separate requirements. This result shows that, read as statements about all the modes of the horizon together, they are one. The geometry part can be made local: near any point, however strong the gravitational field is, the smoothness condition that sets the temperature at a black hole gives the Unruh temperature, up to small corrections. For a quantum state on a finite set of modes, being thermal for a flow and having that flow as its internal clock are the same property. What is left is one assumption, that the modes of every small horizon are jointly thermal at that temperature. At black holes the series makes the corresponding assumption in two parts, one for each mode separately and one for how the modes combine; the local version needs both, so it is a new assumption, stronger than the black-hole smoothness rule alone. It is not derived here from anything weaker.

title: On a horizon generator the weight-$\tfrac12$ scaling preserves the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of a kernel shrunk onto a point, so a gauge-invariant quasi-free state locally normal to the null vacuum at a point is locally the null vacuum there in every regular parameter, and a stationary gauge-invariant quasi-free state locally normal to it at the edge is the null vacuum of (N$_{+}$), positivity included; every other stationary gauge-invariant quasi-free state, the half-thermal products at every period included, is locally disjoint from it at the edge
text: A black hole's horizon is made of light rays, and the series' premise says that the quantum field on those rays is in its lowest-energy state for sliding along them. This result shows that, for a field that does not change in time, that premise is the same as a standard locality requirement of quantum field theory: close to the point where the horizon's light rays begin, the state must look like the vacuum in the strong sense that the two cannot be told apart by measurements in a small enough region. The reason is a scaling property: zooming in by the horizon's own time evolution keeps a measure of the difference from the vacuum exactly unchanged, so a time-independent state that differs from the vacuum at all differs equally at every scale and is distinguishable at the starting point. States that are thermal on each half of the light ray fail at that point, even at the Hawking temperature. The locality requirement is borrowed from the literature, not derived in the series.

title: The imported MacDowell-Mansouri functional, in the series' frozen-point form, is a dynamical principle for the whole gauge field that fixes the trace-free part: its frame equation is twice the dual of $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a$, ten conditions with the Weyl part dropping out, and its restriction to pure dilations is the single Yamabe trace; with the standard (imported) Einstein-Cartan matter coupling its on-shell Schouten tensor is the stored derivative of the scale tractor, so the infinity-vacuum incidence is its vacuum case

Varying it gives all ten equations, with matter entering as an independent source, and when matter is absent it reproduces exactly the series' geometric statement of Einstein's condition. Freezing the light cones in this same action leaves only the one equation found before. The action is taken from the literature rather than derived from the series' transport, and it disagrees with the series' entropy premise about one geometric term in horizon entropy.

title: On a mode space where the boost acts by phases, it dilates no translation group, so the Borchers route to (R) needs the continuum
text: One hope for explaining the black-hole temperature without simply assuming it uses a celebrated theorem: if the time-stretching symmetry at a horizon acts on a family of positive-energy shifts by rescaling them, the temperature comes out automatically with the right value. This result shows that the discrete models the series uses for the horizon's quantum modes cannot host that mechanism: their time evolution only ever returns close to where it started, and a rescaling that never escapes a bounded region can only rescale shifts that do nothing. The mechanism needs a genuinely continuous spectrum of mode energies, so any derivation of the temperature along these lines has to be built on the series' continuum description of the modes.

title: (R$_{\mathrm{loc}}$), with the local-horizon modes labelled by null direction, is independent of the present premises, and what it adds off Killing horizons is the matter coupling; a local rapidity period $2\pi c$ gives Einstein's equations with $G_{\mathrm{cl}} = cG$

This result shows the temperature assumption is extra, given the series' present assumptions: one can keep everything else the series says, including everything about black holes and the cosmological horizon, and give the tiny horizons, with their modes labelled by the light-like direction they belong to, a different temperature, and nothing breaks. What changes is the strength of gravity felt by ordinary matter. If tiny horizons were half as warm as assumed, matter would gravitate twice as strongly as the black-hole formulas say. title: The light-ray arrays of the slot-module matter are its Weyl components, sixteen per generation for every CPT halving and every mass term, so a generation registers eight units of ln 2; the particle half is chiral in every halving, so the counted species are not gauge-covariant Dirac species, and with a nonzero Majorana term not Dirac species by mass either
text: The series counts quantum ladders on a black hole's horizon, and a counted unit has to be two ladders. An earlier result showed that one electron-like particle, which comes in two handednesses, supplies exactly two ladders, and the open question was whether every counted particle is of that kind. This result counts the particles the series itself predicts, one generation of sixteen handed components from its slot construction. Each component supplies one ladder whatever its mass, so a generation gives sixteen ladders, eight units, a whole number. But the series' matter is handed: almost no component has a mirror partner with the same charges, so the particles cannot be grouped into two-handed ones in a way the forces respect, and with the series' neutrino mass the neutrinos are one-handed. The count works; the reason offered for it does not.

title: On a horizon generator the boost is the anticommutator-preserving scaling about the edge, so a stationary gauge-invariant quasi-free state is its own scaling limit there and is the null vacuum of (N$_{+}$) exactly when it is locally the null vacuum at the edge; stationary states thermal on each half at any period, with or without cross-edge correlation, are locally the null vacuum at every other point, so the content of (N$_{+}$) beyond stationarity sits at the bifurcation surface alone
text: The series assumes that the quantum modes along a horizon's light rays are in their lowest-energy state for sliding along the rays, and from that it gets the horizon's temperature. This result asks where that assumption really bites. A black hole in equilibrium does not change in time, and on the horizon's light rays "not changing in time" turns out to mean "looking the same at every magnification about the point where the two halves of the horizon meet". So if the state looks like empty space at very short distances at that one meeting point, it looks like empty space everywhere along the ray, and the assumption holds. At every other point of the ray, a state at the wrong temperature, or at zero temperature, also looks like empty space at short distances; only the meeting point tells them apart. So any deeper principle that would explain the black-hole temperature must say something about that meeting point, which lies outside the single map of spacetime the series uses for the black hole.

This framework puts its quantum structure deep inside the hole instead, so it predicts no echoes: the ringing should be exactly as general relativity says. A single confirmed echo would refute it.

text:
The thread runs from a dictionary with Einstein's theory, through two routes to his equations, to the quantum state on the horizon that the first route needs. [[t]]

Each route rests on premises. [[t]] The horizon route assumes (C$_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and the Clausius relation, and (Loc) is not derived. [[c:synthesis.c-loc-local-horizon-premise]] The action route assumes the field-space premise (FS). [[c:synthesis.field-space-premise-parallel-frozen-point]] Einstein's rule that the whole stress is the source is not given by gauge invariance; it is the trace-free channel, which the horizon route takes through its null fluxes. [[c:synthesis.weyl-flat-variations-carry-only-the-stress-trace-and-the-whole-stress-clause-is-the-trace-free-channel]] The temperature comes from (N$_{+}$), whose local form is now a theorem for Hadamard states of the Dirac field. [[c:synthesis.hadamard-scaling-limit-premise]] That the series' own state is Hadamard is a further premise, (HD): the state the descent leaves is Hadamard on a Cauchy collar, and propagation carries that to every later field. [[c:synthesis.hadamard-deposit-premise]]

Three things stay open. [[t]] The strength of gravity has no route free of a fitted cut-off. [[c:synthesis.series-content-induces-a-newton-coupling-only-through-an-unfixed-cut-off]] The ground-state clause of (N$_{+}$) is not derived, since local conditions give only the vacuum's family. [[c:synthesis.normality-on-the-closed-generator-gives-the-vacuum-folium-not-the-ground-state]] Nothing in the series yet selects which Hadamard state the world is in.
